questions.prompt: Let $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^3$ be a differentiable function such that $(Df)(0,0)$ has rank 2. Write $f=(f_1,f_2,f_3)$. Which statements are necessarily true?

options.A: f is injective in a neighbourhood of (0,0).
options.B: There exists an open neighbourhood U of (0,0) in R² such that f₃ is a function of f₁ and f₂.
options.C: f maps an open neighbourhood of (0,0) in R² onto an open subset of R³.
options.D: (0,0) is an isolated point of f⁻¹({f(0,0)}).

hints: Rank 2 gives an injective linear derivative, but the inverse function theorem needs continuity of the derivative near the point.
A first-order lower bound isolates the fiber; oscillating derivatives can still destroy injectivity between other nearby points.
questions.solution: Under the literal printed hypothesis, only D is necessary. Let L=Df(0); rank 2 means L is injective, so on the unit circle min||Lh||=m>0. Differentiability gives f(h)−f(0)=Lh+r(h), with ||r(h)||/||h||→0. For sufficiently small nonzero h, ||f(h)−f(0)||≥(m/2)||h||>0, proving D. A fails: define g(0)=0, g(x)=x+x²sin(1/x²) for x≠0 and f(x,y)=(g(x),y,0). This map is differentiable everywhere and Df(0) has rank 2. Yet g′(x)=1+2xsin(1/x²)−(2/x)cos(1/x²) has both positive and negative values in every interval about 0 (use x=(2πn)^(-1/2) and x=((2n+1)π)^(-1/2)). A continuous injection on an interval is strictly monotone and cannot have derivatives of both signs, so f is not injective on any neighborhood. B fails for f(x,y)=(x,0,y): f₃ cannot be determined by (f₁,f₂)=(x,0). C fails for f(x,y)=(x,y,0), whose image lies in a plane. The NTA final key gives options 1 and 4. Those are valid if the missing stronger hypothesis f∈C¹ is imposed: choose two components whose derivative minor is invertible and apply the inverse function theorem. The printed source says only differentiable, so this record is marked source_issue with no graded options rather than silently strengthening the premise.
questions.theory: The inverse function theorem normally assumes a C¹ map on a neighborhood and an invertible derivative at the point. For a C¹ map from R² to R³ of rank 2 at the origin, some two-component projection has an invertible 2×2 derivative, yielding a local coordinate chart and local injectivity of the full map. Merely having a derivative at every point does not provide its continuity, so this argument is unavailable as printed. Differentiability at the one point nevertheless controls its own fiber: the injective linear approximation has a positive lower bound on unit vectors, and the smaller remainder cannot cancel it. This distinguishes isolation of f⁻¹(f(0)) from injectivity between arbitrary nearby points. Also rank 2 does not specify which pair of components forms coordinates; f₁ and f₂ may have a singular derivative even if another pair works. An immersed two-dimensional surface in R³ does not contain a three-dimensional open set locally. The official answer reflects the usual C¹ theorem, and that extra assumption must be identified explicitly.

similar_questions.prompt: Suppose f:R²→R³ is C¹ and Df(0) has rank 2. Prove local injectivity.
similar_questions.solution: Select two rows of Df(0) giving a nonsingular 2×2 minor, and let F be the corresponding two-component map. The C¹ inverse function theorem gives a neighborhood where F is one-to-one. If f(p)=f(q) there, then F(p)=F(q), forcing p=q. Thus f is locally injective.

similar_questions.prompt: If f is only differentiable at 0 and Df(0) is injective, prove 0 is isolated in f⁻¹(f(0)).
similar_questions.solution: Compactness of the unit sphere gives ||Df(0)h||≥m||h|| for m>0. The differentiability remainder is ≤m||h||/2 near 0. Thus ||f(h)−f(0)||≥m||h||/2>0 for every sufficiently small h≠0. This proves fiber isolation without claiming local injectivity.

questions.prompt: Let $\varnothing\neq K\subseteq\mathbb R$ and let $f:K\to K$ be continuous with $|x-y|\leq|f(x)-f(y)|$ for all $x,y\in K$. Which statements are true?

options.B: f must be surjective if K=[0,1].
options.C: f is injective and f⁻¹:f(K)→K is continuous.
options.D: f is injective, but f⁻¹:f(K)→K need not be continuous.

hints: If f(x)=f(y), the lower distance bound forces x=y.
The inverse is 1-Lipschitz. On [0,1], compare the images of the endpoints.
questions.solution: If f(x)=f(y), then |x−y|≤0 and x=y, proving injectivity. For s=f(x),t=f(y), the same inequality gives |f⁻¹(s)−f⁻¹(t)|≤|s−t|; the inverse is 1-Lipschitz and hence continuous, proving C and disproving D. A is true: on K=[0,∞), f(x)=x+1 preserves distances and is continuous but misses [0,1). For K=[0,1], |f(1)−f(0)|≥1, and both images lie in [0,1], forcing the images to be 0 and 1 in some order. By continuity and the intermediate value theorem f attains every value in [0,1], proving B. Correct: A,B,C.
questions.theory: A distance-expanding map satisfies d(x,y)≤d(f(x),f(y)); equality is permitted, so isometries are included. This directly implies injectivity and gives a 1-Lipschitz inverse on the image, with no need to assume differentiability. A Lipschitz map is uniformly continuous because the same distance threshold works everywhere. Surjectivity does not follow on arbitrary noncompact sets: translation can move an infinite ray into a proper subset while preserving distances. On the compact interval [0,1], the diameter is 1. The distance between the endpoint images must equal that maximum, so the images are opposite endpoints; continuity then fills the intervening interval. The inverse domain is f(K), not automatically all of K until surjectivity has been established. Distinguish expansion of distances from contraction: it is the inverse whose Lipschitz constant is at most one.

similar_questions.prompt: On K=R define f(x)=2x. Verify the inequality and determine the inverse’s Lipschitz constant.
similar_questions.solution: |f(x)−f(y)|=2|x−y|≥|x−y|. The map is onto R and its inverse is s/2, with Lipschitz constant 1/2.

similar_questions.prompt: On K=[0,∞), does f(x)=x+2 satisfy the hypotheses and is it onto?
similar_questions.solution: It is continuous and |f(x)−f(y)|=|x−y|. Its image is [2,∞), so it is not onto K. The inverse on this image is s−2 and is 1-Lipschitz.
